title: What Happens When You Open a Website?

sources.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names — Concepts and Facilities
sources.notes: Checked resolver, hierarchy and cache behavior; narrative uses a deliberately simplified uncached lookup.

sources.title: RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1
sources.notes: Checked request/response framing and connection management; this episode uses a teaching example of HTTP/1.1 over TCP.

sources.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol
sources.notes: Checked ports, sequence numbers and connection establishment.

sources.title: RFC 9114: HTTP/3
sources.notes: Checked HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC rather than TCP.

sections.title: One click, many conversations
sections.narration: A click starts several conversations. Watch our request find a server, cross a local network, and reach another network. Each moving envelope reveals a different communication responsibility.
sections.takeaway: Opening a website is a sequence of coordinated network tasks.

sections.title: Choose a clear teaching model
sections.narration: We will follow HTTP version one point one over TCP. Real browsers can reuse connections, caches, and newer protocols. This simplified first visit makes the hidden steps visible.
sections.takeaway: This example explains one path, not every modern browser connection.

sections.title: From LAN to WAN
sections.narration: The browser starts on a local network. Routers connect that network to others. Follow the request across those boundaries: the Internet is an interconnection of separate networks.
sections.takeaway: The Internet connects many separate networks.

sections.title: Layers divide the work
sections.narration: OSI names seven conceptual layers. Our four-layer TCP/IP model combines application functions and groups physical transmission with local-link delivery. Watch the corresponding responsibilities converge without assuming identical implementations.
sections.takeaway: OSI and TCP/IP group related communication responsibilities differently.

sections.title: Ask for an address
sections.narration: The browser knows a name, not necessarily an address. It asks a resolver for DNS information. Follow the query outward and the resulting address back toward the browser.
sections.takeaway: DNS helps translate a useful name into addressing information.

sections.title: Follow the DNS hierarchy
sections.narration: An uncached resolver can follow referrals from root to top-level domain to authoritative server. Each answer points toward more specific information; the laptop usually delegates this work to its resolver.
sections.takeaway: An uncached DNS lookup may follow several referrals.

sections.title: Reuse a cached answer
sections.narration: A cached answer can shorten the next lookup. Watch the resolver return it directly while its lifetime remains valid. The timer shows why cached information cannot be reused indefinitely.
sections.takeaway: A cached DNS answer can shorten the next visit.

sections.title: Choose the receiving process
sections.narration: The destination IP reaches the host. A transport port helps select the endpoint there. Our client uses source port forty-nine thousand one hundred fifty-two and destination port eighty.
sections.takeaway: An IP address alone does not select the receiving application.

sections.title: Establish a TCP connection
sections.narration: The client sends SYN, the server returns SYN with an acknowledgment, and the client acknowledges. These messages establish TCP state; they do not reserve a dedicated Internet circuit.
sections.takeaway: The TCP handshake establishes connection state at both ends.

sections.title: Build the HTTP request
sections.narration: Now send GET for the desired resource. HTTP gives the request its application meaning. TCP carries its bytes without interpreting what the browser wants from the server.
sections.takeaway: HTTP describes what the application wants.

sections.title: Wrap the application bytes
sections.narration: Keep watching the same blue message. Lower layers add their own information around it. That packaging is encapsulation; one large application message may span several transport segments.
sections.takeaway: Encapsulation packages one layer's data for the next layer.

sections.title: Transport adds its information
sections.narration: The transport envelope adds ports and sequence information. The original HTTP bytes remain inside. TCP organizes a stream, so its segments need not match the application's original writes.
sections.takeaway: TCP organizes a byte stream into segments for transmission.

sections.title: Address the IP packet
sections.narration: The next envelope adds source and destination IP information. Routers use destination information to forward hop by hop. The destination normally remains the server, although address translation can change addresses.
sections.takeaway: IP addressing supports delivery across interconnected networks.

sections.title: Prepare the local frame
sections.narration: The outer link envelope serves this local hop. For a remote server, its next destination may be the gateway's interface. Local MAC addressing and distant IP addressing answer different questions.
sections.takeaway: A link-layer frame serves one local link.

sections.title: Turn bits into signals
sections.narration: Bits are encoded as physical signals, not little written numerals moving through a cable. Watch the bit pattern become changing signal levels; electrical, optical, and radio links encode differently.
sections.takeaway: Physical transmission carries encoded information over a medium.

sections.title: The switch forwards a frame
sections.narration: The switch forwards a frame toward the appropriate local port using MAC forwarding information. Its job differs from selecting an IP route between networks. Follow the chosen branch.
sections.takeaway: A switch forwards within its link-layer domain.

sections.title: The router chooses a next hop
sections.narration: The router removes the incoming link envelope, examines the IP destination, and chooses an outgoing next hop. It need not understand the HTTP request to forward ordinary traffic.
sections.takeaway: Routers connect networks by forwarding IP packets.

sections.title: New frame, continuing packet
sections.narration: Watch the outer frame change at each routed hop while the destination IP continues toward the server. Different local links can use different addresses and transmission technologies.
sections.takeaway: Link-layer envelopes are replaced as a packet crosses routers.

sections.title: Shared links can queue or lose
sections.narration: Shared outgoing links have finite capacity. Packets queue while others leave, and a full queue can drop arrivals. The moving backlog adds delay beyond transmission and propagation alone.
sections.takeaway: Packets share limited resources along the path.

sections.title: Unwrap at the server
sections.narration: At the server, processing moves upward. Remove the local envelope, process IP and TCP information, then deliver the available HTTP bytes. Each receiving layer handles its own information.
sections.takeaway: Decapsulation lets each receiving layer perform its own job.

sections.title: Send an HTTP response
sections.narration: The server sends status information, headers, and content back through the layers. Follow the return traffic. Its route need not exactly match the path taken by the request.
bullets: The response takes a return path
sections.takeaway: The server sends a new application message back.

sections.title: A page can trigger more requests
sections.narration: The first HTML response can name more resources. Watch separate requests fetch styles and images. A visible page can require many transfers, some served by caches or different servers.
sections.takeaway: One visible page can require many resource transfers.
sections.short_title: Fetch the rest of the page

sections.title: Add the modern distinctions
sections.narration: HTTPS adds TLS protection. HTTP version three uses QUIC over UDP rather than this TCP example. The protocol combination changes, but addressing, forwarding, and physical transmission still matter.
sections.takeaway: The web uses several protocol combinations, not only HTTP over TCP.

sections.title: Retell the whole journey
sections.narration: We found addressing information, established our example's connection, requested a resource, crossed networks, and unpacked the response. Now distinguish the name, IP address, transport port, and local envelope yourself.
sections.takeaway: A page load succeeds because multiple protocols perform distinct jobs.
